prompt.context: Our client is Prospect Equity Partners ('Prospect'), a prominent Private Equity firm that invests in the technology space. They have recently acquired Events.com due to strong commercial wins and momentum in the market. Events.com is a leading SaaS-based registration/ticketing platform for Endurance events (5K runs, Marathons, Triathlons, Mud Runs, etc.). They make money by taking registrations and processing payments for events and charging a fee per transaction — similar to Ticketmaster or Eventbrite (e.g., $100 registration price x 10% Fee = $10 in Revenue for Events.com). Events.com has doubled market share since 2015, but in the last two years revenue is flat and profits are down, despite growing share.
prompt.question: Prospect wants you to determine what is causing the decline in profitability and come up with a plan to improve it.

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: Two main other players: Active Network and RunSignUp. No recent entrants.
All in the US. Historically, local 5K events are targeted, but Events.com recently signed IRONMAN triathlon in Q4 2017, which has $125M in transaction volume per year, and other premium events.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to the overall market?
clarifying_info.a: The market has declined ~4% per year since 2015, driven by low participation in experiential runs like Color or Mud Runs.
The platform is called EventWorks Endurance and has been around for 10+ years.

clarifying_info.q: Have there been any changes to the company since acquisition?
clarifying_info.a: No changes have been made to the company since being acquired by Prospect.

exhibits.title: Historical P&L and Market Share
exhibits.shows: A P&L table (2015–2018) with Revenue, Variable Costs (Payment Processing, Server Hosting), Fixed Costs (Headcount, Marketing, SG&A), and Operating Income/Margin; plus two pie charts showing market share in 2015 and 2018 among Events.com, Active Network, RunSignUp, and Other.

exhibits.title: Payment Processing Breakdown
exhibits.shows: A table comparing 2017 and 2018 on: number of events, total registrations, dollars processed, Events.com Revenue, and Payment Processing Expenses.

exhibits.title: Pricing Structure
exhibits.shows: A comparison of the old and new pricing structures: old structure had a single 10% fee per transaction; new structure uses a tiered fixed fee ($3.00 for registrations under $50; $5.50 for registrations over $50).

framework: Analyze profitability: review P&L for revenue vs. cost trends, identify which cost line is driving margin compression

Identify root cause: isolate whether the payment processing cost increase is driven by rate (price per dollar processed) or volume (dollars processed); then decompose revenue into fee rate and average registration price
Quantify impact: calculate the revenue/profit effect of the pricing structure change and size the opportunity from a pricing fix
Recommend: propose specific pricing change, quantify the improvement, and flag risks and next steps

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit A, what is driving the decline in profitability from 2017 to 2018?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note revenue is flat at $39.9M while operating income fell from $17.6M to $13.5M (~$4.1M decline). Fixed costs are largely stable. The key mover is Payment Processing Costs jumping from $8.0M to $11.9M (+$3.9M). Server hosting and fixed costs show only minor changes. Candidate should hypothesize the payment processing spike is due to either higher processing volume or a higher processing rate, and ask for Exhibit B.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit B, is the payment processing cost increase driven by rate or volume? Also calculate the average fee rate and average price per registration for 2017 and 2018.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the payment processing rate (cost/dollars processed) to test rate vs. volume. Both years show ~2%, confirming rate is unchanged — the cost increase is volume-driven. Next, the candidate should compute the average fee rate (Revenue / Dollars Processed) and average price per registration (Dollars Processed / Registrations). The average price per registration nearly doubled while fee rate fell sharply, pointing to a pricing structure change as the root cause.

math.setup: Processing rate = Payment Processing Expenses / Dollars Processed; Avg fee rate = Revenue / Dollars Processed; Avg price per registration = Dollars Processed / Registrations
steps: Processing rate 2018: $11.9M / $595M ≈ 2% — rate is unchanged, cost increase is volume-driven
Avg fee rate 2018: $39.9M / $595M ≈ 6.7% — fee rate dropped sharply
Avg price per registration 2018: $595M / 7.9M ≈ $75 — average registration price increased ~50%
math.answer: Processing rate held steady at ~2%; volume drove cost increase. Average fee rate fell from 10% to 6.7%. Average price per registration rose from ~$50 to ~$75, indicating higher-value events (like IRONMAN) now dominate volume.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit C, explain how the pricing change caused revenue to be flat despite higher transaction volume, and quantify the revenue impact of adding a 2.25% credit card surcharge to the 'Over $50' tier.
questions.guidance: Candidate should see that the old 10% variable fee on a ~$50 average registration yielded ~$5/registration. The new fixed $5.50 fee for over-$50 registrations (like $75 IRONMAN registrations) yields only $5.50 vs. what would have been $7.50 under the old model — so revenue is capped by the fixed fee as average prices rise. Candidate should then calculate the incremental revenue from adding a 2.25% fee to the ~$375M of over-$50 volume. Exact calculation required — no rounding.

recommendation: Events.com changed its pricing model from a 10% variable fee to a tiered fixed fee structure; as high-value events (like IRONMAN at ~$75/registration) replaced lower-value customers, the fixed $5.50 cap meant revenue stayed flat while payment processing costs rose with dollar volume

Recommend adding a 2.25% variable 'Credit Card Fee' to the Over $50 pricing tier, which customer surveys indicate can be implemented with negligible customer losses — this will add approximately $8.4M in revenue and operating income annually
risks: Additional increases in average price per registration could erode margins further if fixed fees are not adjusted
Customers (event organizers) may react negatively to future pricing changes or seek alternatives (RunSignUp has grown market share significantly)
The overall endurance events market is declining ~4% per year, limiting long-term growth
next_steps: Design and execute roll-out strategy for the 2.25% credit card fee addition
Investigate additional pricing tier adjustments to protect against further increases in average registration price (e.g., add a third tier for registrations over $100)
Conduct customer and market research to determine willingness to pay and optimal pricing thresholds
Evaluate targeting lower-priced event segments to rebalance the mix
Consider acquiring RunSignUp to consolidate market position and stratify product offerings
Assess whether to exit the declining endurance market or pivot to adjacent verticals
